content:
I've been thinking about fatherhood. Not in the abstract way people mean when they say they want children someday, the way they say they want to learn Italian or see Patagonia - a pleasant intention floating somewhere in the future without urgency. In the concrete sense. The sense that lands in your body and rearranges your priorities before your mind has caught up with it.

I want a child. I want to be a father. And I'm terrified by what that means in this particular moment of history.

The terror is specific, and I suspect it's shared by more people my age than the birth rate statistics manage to convey.

I can see the world changing. I've spent years watching the curves - energy, AI, geopolitics, the institutional decay I've written about at length - and the curves tell me the world my child would inherit will be fundamentally different from the one I grew up in. Not slightly different, and not different in the way each generation experiences difference. Different the way the world before and after the printing press was different, or before and after electrification.

The skills that served me may be worthless to my child. The institutions I navigated may not exist. The career paths, the educational frameworks, the social arrangements - all of it is in flux and the flux is accelerating.

What do you teach someone whose future you genuinely cannot predict?

The question is practical, and every prospective parent in my generation faces it whether or not they put it into words. The previous generation could prepare children for a world resembling the one they knew. My parents could reasonably assume the skills and values and strategies that worked for them would work in modified form for me. The assumption was imperfect and it was functional, which was enough.

I can't make it. The world that exists when my child reaches adulthood is uncertain enough that any specific preparation risks being precisely wrong - training them for jobs that won't exist, teaching skills that will be automated, readying them for institutions that will have transformed past recognition.

And yet the terror sits alongside something else, something I find difficult to name and that feels more fundamental. A pull. A gravity. The sense that this is what I'm supposed to do, not in any cosmic or teleological way but in the biological, emotional, deeply human way where the desire for children isn't a preference to be weighed against other preferences. It's a different category of thing entirely, and it runs deeper than the rational analysis I'm trained to apply to everything else.

Chronic illness has shaped this in ways I'm still working out. When your body imposes limits most people never encounter, when pain structures your existence enough to make planning difficult and spontaneity dangerous, you develop an unusual relationship with time. You know more viscerally than most people your age that time is finite. That the window for certain experiences doesn't stay open indefinitely. That the body you're in isn't a reliable instrument, and whatever you're going to do you should do before the instrument fails more comprehensively than it already has.

Call it clarity. The cluster headaches have given me a great many things I didn't ask for, and one of them is an acute awareness that life doesn't wait for optimal conditions. There's no perfect moment to become a parent. There's only the moment you're standing in, with whatever uncertainty it contains, and the choice to act inside it or defer indefinitely and call the deferral prudence.

**Watching Other People's Fathers**

I've travelled to forty-five countries, and in a lot of them I watched parents. Not deliberately at first, then increasingly with attention as the question moved from abstract to urgent.

In Japan I watched fathers on the trains, their children immaculate in school uniforms, the interaction marked by an attentiveness I found genuinely moving. The seriousness with which childhood was treated. The investment in the next generation visible in the daily texture of family life rather than only in policy.

In parts of Southeast Asia I watched children growing up in conditions Australians would call deprivation, and I watched them thrive - connected, engaged, resilient, embedded in extended family networks with a density of human contact that Australian suburban life can't match. The material conditions were worse. The relational conditions were, in some ways, better.

In Scandinavia I watched societies organised around the principle that children are a collective responsibility. Parental leave measured in years rather than weeks. Universal, affordable childcare. Public space designed for families. The assumption built into policy and culture that raising the next generation warrants genuine societal investment.

And in Australia I watch a country where housing costs consume enough income that starting a family requires either inherited wealth or a tolerance for financial precariousness. Where childcare rivals a mortgage payment. Where work culture assumes an availability incompatible with attentive parenting. Where the birth rate falls year after year because the material conditions for raising children deteriorate while the rhetoric about family values continues unchanged.

**What I Can Actually Give**

The question I keep returning to has stopped being whether to become a father, which is decided. It's what kind, and what I give a child growing up in a world I can't predict.

Not skills specifically, because skills become obsolete. Not knowledge specifically, because knowledge became searchable. Something else, harder to name and much harder to teach.

Judgement. The ability to assess a situation without a manual - to read a room or a market or a moment and know what's required without being told. This resists automation because it depends on context, and context is what machines handle worst.

Resilience, and I mean the real version rather than the motivational poster one about bouncing back. The ability to keep functioning under sustained uncertainty without collapsing into denial or despair. I know something about this. The headaches taught me brutally and without my consent.

And the capacity to find meaning in the absence of guarantees, which is what I've taken from chronic illness and from travel and from honestly examining systems that claim to work and don't. Meaning isn't given. It's constructed, and construction is a skill that can be practised, developed, and I believe passed on.

I don't know what world my child will live in. I know it will differ from mine in ways I can't fully imagine. What I can offer is the capacity to navigate whatever arrives rather than preparation for any specific version of it.

That, and the knowledge - which I hope they feel long before they can put words to it - that they were wanted. Not as an accessory or an obligation or a default. Wanted fiercely and deliberately, by someone who could see the storm coming and chose to bring them into it anyway, because the storm was never the whole story, and because the world, even this one, even now, holds enough beauty and strangeness and possibility to justify the risk.

Because life, even uncertain life, even painful life, is the thing itself. And wanting to share it with someone new is the deepest form of optimism I know how to practise.
